newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung won't strangle Hong Kong, says politician.
newsitem.headline: Tung won't strangle Hong Kong, says politician.

text.p: A pro-China political leader in Hong Kong denied on Tuesday that the territory's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, would strangle Hong Kong with his plans to curb civil and political liberties.
"Tung Chee-hwa is not trying to strangle human rights here," politician Maria Tam said in a speech to the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.

Hong Kong, a British colony for 156 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30 with a pledge that its 6.4 million people can keep their economic and political way of life unchanged for a further 50 years after the handover.
Under Tung's plan, launched three weeks ago, foreign donations to local political parties would be banned and demonstrations would require police permission.

Tam, a leading member of China's Preparatory Committee, which is charged with setting up the post-handover political system, said similar restrictions existed in the United States, Canada, Australia and other Western states.
Tam said the move did not mean that political liberty in the territory would be curtailed after China takes over.

"We are not the most liberal, but nor are we the most restricted place in the world," said Tam, also a member of the China-backed provisional legislature that will replace the current elected Legislative Council, which is to be disbanded.
Tam said it was necessary to amend some current laws, even though the liberal laws had created no instability in the colony.
Until now, demonstrations in Hong Kong were not directed against sovereign Britain or the Queen, Tam said.
Most protests in Hong Kong are directed against Beijing, the future sovereign. Tam declined to speculate on whether there would be mass protests against China after Beijing resumes control.
